strengths: Clear and well-motivated theoretical framework: the attention-matching objective is grounded in an exact decomposition of concatenated-block attention into locally normalized outputs weighted by attention mass (Eq. 5, Appendix A.2), giving a principled justification for why matching both attention output and attention mass (via the novel bias term) is sufficient for compatibility with future KV-cache concatenation.

The method decomposes into simple, closed-form subproblems (NNLS for bias, least squares for values, greedy/heuristic selection for keys), enabling compaction in seconds-to-minutes rather than the GPU-hours required by Cartridges, while achieving comparable or better downstream accuracy at practical compaction ratios (up to 50x).

Extensive empirical evaluation across three model families (Qwen3-4B, Llama3.1-8B, Gemma3-12B) and two distinct long-context benchmarks (QuALITY, LongHealth), with comparisons against a wide range of relevant baselines (Cartridges, H2O+, SnapKV, PyramidKV, KVzip, summarization variants, DuoAttention).

Thorough ablation studies (leave-one-out analysis in Fig. 4, reference-query sampling comparison in Appendix D, aggregation function comparison in Appendix F.1) that isolate the contribution of each design choice.

Interesting and practically useful finding that per-head attention sensitivity is largely input-invariant, enabling a reusable, precomputed nonuniform compaction schedule per model (Section 3.4, Figs. 2, 6-8), with an accompanying explanation for why sliding-window architectures retain performance under aggressive compaction.

Strong reproducibility: extensive appendices detail exact algorithms (OMP variants, NNLS solver, chunked compaction implementations), hyperparameters, and wall-clock timing breakdowns per computational stage (Table 1).

Nice practical extensions demonstrating versatility: combining Attention Matching with summarization for ~200x compaction (Table 2), and a preliminary but promising online/mid-trajectory compaction experiment on AIME showing preserved reasoning ability under repeated compaction (Appendix F.3).
weaknesses: Evaluation is restricted to models up to 12B parameters and largely to multiple-choice QA benchmarks (QuALITY, LongHealth); there is no evaluation on open-ended generation, summarization faithfulness, or agentic/coding tasks that motivate the paper's framing (e.g., Claude Code/Codex compaction), leaving significance for the stated real-world use cases somewhat unproven.

The Cartridges baseline may be undertrained/under-tuned relative to its original configuration (the paper itself notes 'additional Cartridges training may further improve its results'), which could bias the headline comparison at extreme compaction ratios in the paper's favor; a more carefully matched compute budget or convergence check would strengthen the claim.

Compaction time, while much faster than Cartridges, is still on the order of minutes for the best-performing OMP variant on long documents, and query generation (self-study/repeat-prefill) dominates runtime with limited discussion of how much this could realistically be optimized in production settings.

The key-selection step (restricting Ck to a subset of original keys) lacks a closed-form or theoretically justified solution and is acknowledged by the authors as a source of the performance gap versus Cartridges at very high (100x) compaction ratios, indicating the method's degradation is not fully explained or resolved.

The nonuniform head-budget procedure relies on an approximate separability assumption (single-head sensitivity curves measured with other heads fixed) that is not rigorously validated for potential interaction effects between heads, and its benefits are demonstrated mainly through perplexity ablations rather than downstream task metrics.

The paper introduces many interacting design choices (query sampling strategy, key selection method, bias stabilization heuristics, chunking strategy, nonuniform budgeting) that make the overall system feel like an engineering pipeline with many tunable knobs, which may reduce clarity about which components are essential versus incidental, despite the ablation study.

Some empirical results undercut the primary claims: KVzip sometimes matches or exceeds Attention Matching performance (Figure 3), which is attributed post-hoc to its nonuniform budget advantage rather than being investigated or addressed directly.

strengths: Well-motivated theoretical derivation: the paper shows that preserving both locally-normalized attention output and attention mass for a compacted block is sufficient to approximately preserve full attention behavior under arbitrary future concatenation (Eq. 1-2, Appendix A.2), which is a clean and useful insight that generalizes the token-eviction paradigm by adding a principled bias correction term.

The method decomposes into closed-form/convex subproblems (NNLS for bias fitting, least squares for value fitting), enabling compaction in seconds-to-minutes rather than the GPU-hours required by Cartridges, while achieving comparable or better downstream accuracy at practical (e.g., 50x) compaction ratios — this is a compelling systems-relevant Pareto improvement (Figure 1, Figure 4).

Extensive empirical validation across three model families (Qwen3-4B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma3-12B) and five benchmarks (QuALITY, LongHealth, QASPER, LongBench v2, RULER), consistently outperforming a wide range of strong baselines (H2O+, SnapKV, PyramidKV, KVzip, KVMerger, summarization, and Cartridges).

Thorough ablation study (Figure 5, leave-one-out) isolating the contribution of each design choice (biases, learned values, nonuniform head budgets, on-policy/self-study queries), providing good evidence that each component matters.

Nonuniform head-budget analysis is a nice empirical contribution: sensitivity curves are shown to be largely input-invariant and transferable across datasets (Figure 3, Appendix E), motivating a practical one-time precomputed allocation scheme.

Strong reproducibility support: detailed appendices document algorithmic choices (OMP variants, NNLS solvers, numerical stabilization of β), chunked compaction implementation, self-study prompts, and baseline configurations.

Thoughtful discussion of practical deployment considerations (compatibility with GQA/sliding-window/tensor parallelism, incompatibility with MLA, disaggregated/asynchronous compaction) and honest limitations discussion including cases where Cartridges still wins at extreme (100x) compaction.
weaknesses: The mixture decomposition justification (Appendix A.2) relies on an approximate mass-weighted mixture identity that is exact only if attention output and mass are both matched jointly and exactly; since matching is approximate (via least-squares fitting on finite reference queries), the analysis does not rigorously bound the resulting end-to-end error, leaving the theoretical guarantees largely heuristic/empirical rather than proven.

Key selection Ck is restricted to a subset of original keys, which is a design choice justified mainly by tractability rather than optimality; the paper does not explore whether directly-optimized (non-subset) compact keys computed via fast approximate methods could close the residual gap with Cartridges at very high compaction ratios (a gap the authors themselves acknowledge exists at 100x on LongHealth).

Statistical rigor of the main results is limited: QuALITY evaluation uses 50 contexts (894 questions) and LongHealth uses only 4 aggregated contexts (400 questions total), with no confidence intervals or significance tests reported for the main accuracy-vs-ratio curves (Figure 4), making it hard to assess robustness of the reported advantage over baselines like KVzip, which sometimes closely tracks AM performance.

The Cartridges comparison, while acknowledged as imperfect (the paper explicitly notes 'additional Cartridges training may further improve its results'), may understate Cartridges' potential performance since training compute/hyperparameters were not extensively tuned for that baseline, which slightly weakens the significance of the 'faster and better' headline claim at some compaction levels.

The fastest, most practical variants (AM-HighestAttnKeys-fast) are somewhat weaker than the best AM-OMP variant, and even AM-OMP-fast still requires ~100s per context (Table 3), while query generation (especially self-study) dominates cost; the actual wall-clock competitiveness in real deployment settings (vs. simpler heuristics) is somewhat less dramatic than the headline 'seconds' framing suggests for the strongest configurations.

The nonuniform head-budget schedule requires a one-time per-model calibration procedure (sensitivity curve estimation + greedy allocation) that adds engineering complexity and must be redone whenever base model or fine-tune changes, which is not deeply analyzed in terms of cost or sensitivity to the calibration dataset choice beyond QuALITY/LongHealth.

strengths: The core Attention Matching formulation is conceptually clean and well justified: the paper shows theoretically (Appendix A.2) that matching local attention output and attention mass at each KV block is sufficient to preserve behavior under concatenation with arbitrary future tokens, which motivates the specific two-part objective (Eqs. 1-2) rather than an ad hoc heuristic.

The decomposition into closed-form subproblems (NNLS for bias, least squares for values, greedy/heuristic selection for keys) is a genuinely useful algorithmic contribution that avoids gradient-based optimization, yielding large wall-clock speedups relative to Cartridges while remaining competitive in quality on several benchmarks.

Evaluation breadth is a real strength: three model families (Qwen3, Llama3.1, Gemma3), multiple compaction ratios, and five datasets (QuALITY, LongHealth, QASPER, LongBench v2, RULER) with several strong baselines (Cartridges, H2O+, SnapKV, PyramidKV, KVzip, KVMerger, summarization).

Extensive ablations (Figure 5) and supporting analyses (head sensitivity curves, reconstruction-vs-accuracy correlation, nonuniform budget analysis) give reasonable insight into which design choices matter, and the appendix provides substantial implementation detail supporting reproducibility.

The nonuniform per-head compaction schedule, motivated by empirically stable head-sensitivity rankings across contexts/datasets, is an interesting and practically useful finding tied to hybrid sliding-window architectures.
weaknesses: The headline speed claim is somewhat misleading: the highest-quality variant (AM-OMP) still takes on the order of several minutes to over ten minutes per context (Table 3: query generation + OMP selection can exceed 700s for a 60k-token context), while the truly 'fast' (<1 minute) variants sacrifice quality; Figure 1's framing of '50x compaction in seconds' applies mainly to the weaker fast variants, and the paper does not clearly reconcile this tension in the abstract/intro.

The Cartridges baseline may be undertrained relative to what the original method is capable of: the authors themselves note only 1 epoch with default settings was used ("additional Cartridges training may further improve its results"), which weakens the strength of the 'orders of magnitude faster while matching/exceeding Cartridges' claim, especially since Cartridges is reported to outperform AM at the most extreme (100x) compaction ratios on LongHealth.

Evaluation scale for some datasets is small and could limit robustness of conclusions: LongHealth uses only 4 contexts total (100 questions each), and Cartridges is only evaluated on a 20-article QuALITY subset for one model family, making some head-to-head comparisons statistically thin; error bars/variance are largely absent from the main results (Figure 4, Tables 1-2), aside from the head-sensitivity curves.

The method for selecting compact keys (Ck) has no closed-form solution and relies on heuristics (highest-attention or greedy OMP) restricted to subsets of the original keys; this is acknowledged as a limitation but means the 'efficient closed-form solutions' framing in the abstract somewhat overstates the extent to which the full pipeline is closed-form, since the most impactful component (key selection) is heuristic/greedy.

Reference-query generation (self-study, repeat-prefill) requires prefilling/decoding on the full original context first, so the approach is not applicable in settings where full KV materialization is itself the bottleneck (e.g., ingesting extremely long streaming context); the chunked-compaction variant that would help here (KV-based chunking) still requires a full prefill pass over the whole document before chunking, limiting the claimed generality for truly long/streaming contexts.

Scaling claims to much larger (e.g., MoE) models are speculative and unverified experimentally — the argument that KV cache size varies little across model scale does not establish that compaction quality or compute cost analysis (e.g., self-study cost, which dominates runtime) will hold at larger scale or with different attention/architectural choices (e.g., MLA is explicitly noted as incompatible).

strengths: The core technical contribution—decomposing the attention-matching objective into a per-token bias fit via NNLS, a closed-form least-squares fit for values, and a subset-selection problem for keys (via highest-attention or OMP)—is elegant and well-justified. Appendix A.2 gives a clean derivation showing why matching both local attention output and attention mass is sufficient to preserve behavior when compacted caches are concatenated with arbitrary future tokens.

Extensive empirical validation across three model families (Qwen3-4B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-3-12B) and five benchmarks (QuALITY, LongHealth, QASPER, LongBench v2, RULER), with numerous baselines (Cartridges, H2O+, SnapKV, PyramidKV, KVzip, KVMerger, summarization). The method consistently forms the Pareto frontier of compaction time vs. quality (Fig. 1, Fig. 4).

Thorough ablation study (Fig. 5, leave-one-out) isolates the contribution of each design choice (attention biases, learned values, nonuniform head budgets, on-policy queries, self-study), showing all components matter and giving readers insight into which pieces are most important.

The nonuniform head-budget analysis (Sec. 3.4, Fig. 3) is a genuinely interesting empirical finding—head sensitivity to compaction is largely input-invariant and can be precomputed once per model, offering insight beyond just a performance trick (e.g., a plausible explanation for the success of sliding-window hybrid architectures).

Strong reproducibility: extensive appendices document algorithmic details (OMP with periodic refits, NNLS via projected gradient descent), exact prompts used for self-study, baseline configurations, and compute budgets, which would substantially aid replication.

Honest and specific limitations discussion: the paper acknowledges that Cartridges can still outperform Attention Matching at more extreme (100x) compaction ratios on some benchmarks, and that OMP-based variants still take minutes rather than seconds, rather than overselling the method as strictly dominant.
weaknesses: The method restricts Ck to a subset of the original keys rather than solving for compact keys directly, since no closed-form solution exists for optimizing Ck in general; this is an important design compromise that somewhat limits the achievable quality (as acknowledged) but is not deeply explored/contrasted quantitatively against direct key optimization.

As shown in Table 3, query generation (self-study, repeat-prefill) dominates wall-clock compaction time, meaning much of the 'fast' claim rests on avoiding gradient-based optimization rather than avoiding forward-pass compute altogether; this nuance could be foregrounded more clearly in the abstract/intro rather than only in Sec. 4.4.

Evaluation is limited to models up to 12B parameters; the claim that results will transfer to much larger MoE models (e.g., Qwen3-235B-A22B) based only on KV-cache-size-per-token comparisons is speculative and untested.

The Cartridges comparison, while compute-matched in order of magnitude, uses default hyperparameters from the original repository and the authors themselves note 'additional Cartridges training may further improve its results,' leaving some ambiguity about how tight the comparison really is at the highest compaction ratios.

Statistical uncertainty (error bars/variance across seeds or context subsets) is largely absent from the main results in Figure 4 and Tables 1–4, aside from the appendix ablation figures; this makes it harder to assess whether some of the closer method comparisons (e.g., vs. KVzip on LongHealth) are robust.

The LongBench v2 evaluation is restricted to a 47-context subset selected post hoc (correct with full context, incorrect without), which, while transparently documented, introduces a potential selection effect that could favor methods that happen to align well with this specific curated distribution.
